query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For equiatomic nanoparticles composed of five or more metals initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution, structural and chemical stability over catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures (473–1923 K) is maintained when high activation barriers for atomic diffusion (i.e. sluggish kinetics) combine with the in situ formation of passivating surface layers to inhibit elemental segregation and oxidation. Conversely, if either kinetic hindrance or surface passivation is insufficient, phase separation and performance degradation will occur.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles of five or more metals in near-equal atomic ratios with a homogeneous single-phase (solid solution) crystal structure.
generation.intervention: Expose these nanoparticles to controlled high-temperature treatments (ranging from 473 to 1923 K) under varying reactive atmospheres (e.g., inert, mildly oxidizing, or reducing conditions).
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in environments with well-controlled gas compositions and heating rates so that intrinsic kinetic factors (sluggish diffusion) and surface chemistry (passivation processes) can be systematically modulated.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale passivating layers (e.g., thin oxides) and the inherent kinetic barriers to atomic migration within the high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution, but at elevated temperatures the balance between mixing enthalpy and diffusion kinetics governs stability. When kinetic barriers slow down atomic rearrangements and surface passivation effectively prevents oxidation, the homogeneous structure is preserved; if not, atoms rearrange leading to phase segregation and structural change.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under optimal kinetic and passivating conditions, nanoparticles will retain a uniform elemental distribution and single-phase solid solution structure, with stable catalytic and thermoelectric performance across the temperature range. In cases where kinetic or passivation effects are compromised, measurable phase separation, compositional inhomogeneity, and a corresponding drop in performance will be observed.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles verified by microscopy and diffraction techniques to be in a homogeneous single-phase state with near-equal elemental distribution prior to temperature treatment.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is expected to hold for nanoparticles with near-equiatomic compositions and may not apply to off-stoichiometric or pre-segregated systems; additionally, extreme oxidizing conditions that rapidly overwhelm passivation could lie outside the valid regime.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature thresholds and environmental parameters at which kinetic stabilization fails are not precisely known and require systematic variation; the influence of specific elemental interactions on surface passivation efficacy also remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize equiatomic nanoparticles via a controlled method to ensure a homogeneous solid solution. Subject the particles to stepwise high-temperature treatments (473–1923 K) under different gas atmospheres (e.g., inert and mildly oxidizing). Use high-resolution TEM, X-ray diffraction, and XPS to monitor any onset of phase segregation or changes in surface chemistry, while simultaneously measuring catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
measurements: Elemental mapping (e.g., using EDS in TEM) before and after high-temperature exposure
Phase identification via XRD to detect any emergent secondary phases
Surface chemical state analysis via XPS to observe passivating layer formation
Performance metrics (catalytic activity, electrical conductivity) under operational conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles retain a uniform single-phase structure and stable performance under conditions where kinetic diffusion or passivation effects are intentionally diminished (e.g., by modifying defect densities or atmosphere composition), or if significant phase segregation is observed despite predicted high kinetic barriers and passivation, the proposed mechanism is falsified.

Toward controllable and predictable synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanocrystals

Abstract: High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanocrystals have attracted extensive attention in catalysis. However, there are no effective strategies for synthesizing them in a controllable and predictable manner. With quinary HEA nanocrystals made of platinum-group metals as an example, we demonstrate that their structures with spatial compositions can be predicted by quantitatively knowing the reduction kinetics of metal precursors and entropy of mixing in the nanocrystals under dropwise addition of the mixing five–metal precursor solution. The time to reach a steady state for each precursor plays a pivotal role in determining the structures of HEA nanocrystals with homogeneous alloy and core-shell features. Compared to the commercial platinum/carbon and phase-separated counterparts, the dendritic HEA nanocrystals with a defect-rich surface show substantial enhancement in catalytic activity and durability toward both hydrogen evolution and oxidation. A map of single-phase high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. Sub-nanometric High-Entropy Alloy Cluster: Hydrogen Spillover Driven Synthesis on CeO2 and Structural Reversibility

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) have attracted significant attention as promising catalysts owing to the various unique synergistic effects originating from the nanometer-scale, near-equimolar mixing of five or more components to produce single-phase solid solutions. However, the study of sub-nanometer HEA clusters having sizes of less than 1 nm remains incomplete despite the possibility of novel functions related to borderline molecular states with discrete quantum energy levels. The present work demonstrates the synthesis of CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs) on which sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters were formed with the aid of a pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on readily reducible CeO2 (110) facets. The CoNiCuZnPd HEA sub-nanoclusters exhibited higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 even at low temperatures compared with the corresponding monometallic catalysts. Stability of high-entropy alloys under electrocatalytic conditions

Abstract: SummaryHigh-entropy alloys are claimed to possess superior stability due to thermodynamic contributions. However, this statement mostly lies on a hypothetical basis. In this study, we use on-line inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer to investigate the dissolution of five representative electrocatalysts in acidic and alkaline media and a wide potential window targeting the most important applications. To address both model and applied systems, we synthesized thin films and carbon-supported nanoparticles ranging from an elemental (Pt) sample to binary (PtRu), ternary (PtRuIr), quaternary (PtRuIrRh), and quinary (PtRuIrRhPd) alloy samples. For certain metals in the high-entropy alloy under alkaline conditions, lower dissolution was observed. Still, the improvement was not striking and can be rather explained by the lowered concentration of elements in the multinary alloys instead of the synergistic effects of thermodynamics.
